controls.summary: Decode expected encodings once into canonical form before validation or other processing.
Encode or escape output at the last step before the target interpreter consumes it.
Use output encoding appropriate to each HTML, XML, CSS, or HTTP header context.
Encode untrusted URL parts for their context and allow only safe URL schemes.
Escape dynamically generated JavaScript and JSON to prevent structural changes.
Parameterize database queries, including queries inside stored procedures.
Use safe argument handling or contextual escaping to prevent OS command injection.
Prevent LDAP injection with query-safe handling of untrusted values.
Use parameterized or precompiled XPath queries.
Sanitize untrusted HTML with a maintained, security-focused library or framework feature.
Avoid dynamic code execution; sanitize user input where execution cannot be avoided.
Allowlist outbound protocols, domains, paths, and ports and sanitize input to prevent SSRF.
Do not build templates from untrusted input without strict validation or sanitization.
Use memory-safe string, copy, and pointer operations to prevent buffer overflows.
Validate signs and ranges to prevent integer overflows.
Release allocated resources and clear freed references to prevent use-after-free.
Disable unsafe XML parser features, including external entity resolution.
Restrict deserialized object types and avoid unsafe deserializers for untrusted data.
Document the expected structures and validation rules for input data.
Document consistency checks between related input values.
Document per-user and application-wide business limits.
Validate input against permitted values, structures, ranges, and business rules.
Enforce validation in a trusted service, not only in the client.
Check related input values together for logical consistency.
Enforce the intended business workflow order for each user without skipped steps.
Enforce documented business limits.
Make business operations atomic: complete every step or restore the prior correct state.
Lock limited resources to prevent double booking under concurrent requests.
Require multiple approvers for high-value business operations.
Limit automated calls that could exhaust resources, quotas, or availability or extract excessive data.
Document required browser security features and behavior when they are unavailable.
Prevent browsers from rendering responses in unintended contexts.
Render plain text with text-only DOM APIs rather than HTML interpreters.
Prevent DOM clobbering through explicit declarations, strict typing, and namespace isolation.
Set Secure on cookies and use the __Secure- prefix when not using __Host-.
Choose SameSite cookie settings to match their purpose and limit cross-site attacks.
Return a Content-Type matching each response body, with a safe charset where applicable.
Do not silently redirect service clients from plaintext HTTP; reserve automatic redirects for browser-facing endpoints.
Ensure users cannot override trusted proxy-provided identity and forwarding headers.
Block HTTP methods that the application does not explicitly support.
Use message signatures for highly sensitive transactions or requests traversing multiple systems.
Ensure intermediaries and servers agree on HTTP message boundaries to prevent request smuggling.
Bound GraphQL query depth, volume, or cost, or allowlist queries to prevent expensive execution.
Disable production GraphQL introspection unless the API is intended for other parties.
Use TLS-protected WebSocket connections.
Validate the WebSocket handshake Origin against allowed origins.
Document permitted upload types, extensions, size limits, and safe handling of malicious files.
Reject files too large to process safely without exhausting service capacity.
Check accepted file extensions and actual content against expected file types.
Bound archive expansion size and entry count before extraction.
Enforce per-user file count and storage quotas.
Reject archive symlinks unless required and confined to an explicit target allowlist.
Prevent uploaded or untrusted generated files from executing as server-side code.
Build file paths from trusted data or strictly validate user names and metadata to prevent traversal and inclusion.
Document anti-automation and rate-limit settings that resist password attacks without enabling malicious lockout.
Document context-specific words that users must not choose as passwords.
Document every authentication path and the required consistent authentication strength.
Require passwords of at least eight characters; prefer a minimum of fifteen.
Allow users to change their passwords.
Require both the current and new password when changing a password.
Document idle and absolute session timeouts and justify departures from NIST reauthentication guidance.
Document the concurrent-session limit and behavior when it is reached.
Document federated session issuers and coordinated expiration, termination, and reauthentication.
Verify session tokens in a trusted backend service.
Use dynamically generated session tokens rather than static API keys.
Generate unique reference session tokens with a CSPRNG and at least 128 bits of entropy.
Document function and object access rules based on caller permissions and resource attributes.
Document field read and write restrictions, including rules dependent on object state.
Document contextual attributes used to make security decisions.
Document contextual risk thresholds and resulting allow, deny, challenge, or step-up decisions.
Require explicit permission for each protected function.
Require permission for each specific object to prevent object-level authorization bypass.
Enforce explicit permissions on individual fields for both reads and writes.
Enforce authorization in a trusted service rather than client-controlled code.
Prevent tenant operations from affecting tenants outside the caller permissions.
Verify a token signature or MAC before trusting self-contained token data.
Allowlist token algorithms and prevent unsigned tokens and symmetric/asymmetric key confusion.
Accept token verification keys only from trusted issuer-specific sources.
Enforce token validity windows, including not-before and expiry claims.
Accept only the token type appropriate to the intended purpose.
Verify that the token audience includes the receiving service.
Send tokens only to components that require them; keep backend-for-frontend tokens on the backend.
Bind unpredictable OAuth transaction secrets to the initiating client, user-agent session, and transaction.
Protect authorization-code token requests against CSRF using PKCE or verified state.
Prevent authorization-server mix-up when the client supports multiple issuers.
Request only the OAuth scopes and permissions that the client needs.
Accept access tokens only when their audience includes the resource server.
Document a standard-based key lifecycle and limit sharing of secret and private keys.
Maintain a current inventory of cryptographic keys, certificates, algorithms, and permitted uses.
Discover encryption, hashing, and signing operations across the system.
Maintain a cryptographic inventory and migration plan for future standards and threats.
Use industry-validated cryptographic implementations.
Permit safe upgrades of cryptographic algorithms, parameters, keys, and encrypted data.
Use cryptographic primitives with at least 128 bits of security.
Handle cryptographic failures securely without creating padding or other error oracles.
Do not use weak block modes or padding schemes.
Authenticate encrypted data to prevent unauthorized modification.
Never reuse a nonce or IV for distinct data encrypted under the same key; generate it as the algorithm requires.
Store passwords using an approved costly password KDF with current security parameters.
Generate unguessable values with a CSPRNG and at least 128 bits of entropy.
Enable only recommended TLS versions and prefer the newest supported version.
Enable recommended cipher suites, preferring the strongest; level 3 requires forward secrecy.
Validate trust in mTLS client certificates before using their identities.
Configure certificate revocation checks such as OCSP stapling.
Enable Encrypted Client Hello to protect handshake metadata.
Require TLS for external HTTP services without plaintext fallback.
Document required communications and user-influenced outbound destinations.
Document connection limits and safe behavior when pools are exhausted.
Document resource release, timeouts, bounded retries, backoff, and failure handling for external services.
Document security-critical secrets and their rotation schedules.
Authenticate backend component communications using individual accounts, short-lived tokens, or certificates.
Use least-privilege accounts for backend component and operating-system communications.
Inventory sensitive data and assign protection levels, including easily decoded token payloads.
Document protection, integrity, retention, logging, privacy, and access requirements for each data class.
Keep secrets and other sensitive values out of URLs and query strings.
Prevent sensitive server-side caching or securely purge cached data after use.
Do not send designated sensitive data to untrusted third parties.
Apply documented encryption, integrity, retention, logging, and privacy controls to sensitive data.
Document risk-based deadlines for component updates and vulnerability remediation.
Maintain a third-party component inventory and verify trusted, maintained package sources.
Document expensive functions and defenses against resource exhaustion and consumer timeouts.
Identify risky third-party libraries in the application documentation.
Document where dangerous functionality is used.
Keep deployed component versions within documented update and remediation deadlines.
Implement documented availability defenses for expensive functions.
Resolve direct and transitive dependencies from intended repositories to prevent dependency confusion.
Allowlist writable fields per controller and action to prevent mass assignment.
Protect shared mutable resources with thread-safe operations and synchronization.
Make resource checks and dependent actions atomic to prevent check/use races.
Inventory logged events, formats, locations, uses, access rules, and retention at every stack layer.
Include enough who, what, where, and when metadata to investigate events.
Synchronize logging clocks and use UTC or explicit timezone offsets.
Send logs only to destinations documented in the logging inventory.
Use log formats that the deployed processor can read and correlate.
Respect data protection levels when logging; omit, mask, or hash sensitive values as required.
Log successful and failed authentication operations and the factors involved.
Log authorization failures; level 3 also records sensitive access and other authorization decisions.
Log documented security events and attempts to bypass security controls.
Log unexpected errors and failed security controls.
Encode untrusted log data to prevent log injection.
Protect logs against unauthorized reading and modification.
Send logs securely to a separate system for analysis, alerting, and escalation.
Return generic sensitive-error responses without stack traces, queries, keys, or tokens.
Remain secure when external resources fail, including during degradation or circuit breaking.
Fail securely and gracefully on exceptions; never continue a transaction after failed security validation.
Provide a final exception handler that preserves error details and prevents whole-process failure.
Restrict TURN relay destinations to non-special-purpose addresses for both IPv4 and IPv6.
Prevent legitimate TURN users from exhausting resources through excessive port allocations.
Protect DTLS certificate keys according to the documented key-management policy.
Configure approved DTLS ciphers and a secure DTLS-SRTP protection profile.
Authenticate SRTP traffic at the media server to prevent injected media and denial of service.
Continue processing media safely when malformed SRTP packets arrive.
